extracted.intended_audience: investigators preparing NIH/NIAID grant applications (e.g., R01, R21)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing the Specific Aims page and associated hypotheses for NIH grant applications (commonly R01), including how to choose number/scope of aims, frame hypotheses, and demonstrate significance, innovation, and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete aims within NOFO timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure you can complete your Aims within the typical timeframe for your chosen Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO). For an R01, that’s typically four to five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design aims that are achievable within the grant period; if they cannot be completed in the timeframe, revise scope or reduce number of aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tackle important research that moves the field forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Your project should tackle important research within your niche: it must be able to move your field forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start broadly with an emphasis on significance. Reviewers ask whether the project addresses an important problem and is likely to exert significant influence on the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support aims with preliminary or published data
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of concepts that can’t be strongly supported with your own preliminary data or published data from other laboratories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposing novel or challenging ideas, include sufficient preliminary data to convince reviewers the approach is plausible; lack of supporting data undermines feasibility and reviewer confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of Specific Aims (avoid over-ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: While you could design a project around two to four Specific Aims, many people create three. Limiting your application to a few Specific Aims keeps you clear of the very common mistake of being overly ambitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proposing less scope that is achievable rather than too much; think small and focused rather than sprawling aims that are unlikely to be completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design aims resilient to single negative outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: A common type of Specific Aim might ask a question like “Does A cause B?” However, your project could come to an end if A doesn’t turn out to cause B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make aims where more than one outcome is of interest (e.g., “Does A cause B or non-B?”) so negative results still generate valuable insights; ensure 'non-B' outcomes make sense with hypothesis and preliminary data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely descriptive aims as main aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Another common type of Specific Aim is descriptive (e.g., measuring levels of X in many samples). Though doable, it is rarely a highly significant finding in itself and often should be avoided unless you have no other choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive work is often better placed in preliminary data; reserve proposal aims for hypothesis-driven, mechanistic, or otherwise impactful experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build aims on your prior experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Like your topic, your Specific Aims should build on your previous experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage demonstrated expertise and prior work to establish credibility and feasibility for the proposed aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative planning integrating aims and experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a gestalt between Aims and Experiments: think about experiments, cost, expertise, and resources while picking aims to ensure impact and feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an iterative process: propose a niche project addressing a significant problem, ensure innovation and uniqueness, outline aims and hypotheses, identify institute/study section, outline experiments, assess feasibility and resources, adjust scope as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address significance, innovation, uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Staying in your niche, propose a project that addresses a highly significant problem, is innovative—can create new knowledge, and is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly articulate Significance and Innovation in the application; reviewers evaluate these attributes when scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check uniqueness using NIH RePORT and other tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Is unique. For details, see What Does NIH Look For?, and search NIH’s RePORT to check whether your project is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use RePORT and related tools to ensure your proposal is not duplicative and to position novelty relative to existing portfolio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify likely funding institute and study section early
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a potential funding institute and a study section that would likely embrace your research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting an appropriate IC and study section helps you tailor aims and presentation to reviewer expertise and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline experiments with clear endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Start broadly with an emphasis on significance, and then focus on generating experiments with clear endpoints reviewers can readily assess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that have measurable, interpretable endpoints; reviewers must be able to see how aims will be tested and evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess feasibility and resource/expertise access
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess feasibility. See whether you have access to all needed resources and expertise. Make sure the project is not growing too big for your targeted time and budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasibility includes personnel, facilities, equipment, and realistic budgeting; if gaps exist, revise aims or secure collaborations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate and revise when encountering roadblocks
rubrics_metrics.description: If you hit a roadblock, go back to the failure point and revise your plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat planning as iterative—re-scope aims, change experiments, or adjust hypotheses when feasibility or conceptual problems arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft Specific Aims and one or more testable hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline draft Specific Aims and one or more hypotheses. You can create one hypothesis for the entire application or one for each Specific Aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis (central or per-aim) anchors aims to a common theme and helps reviewers understand the project's rationale and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make hypotheses well-focused and testable
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong hypothesis should be well-focused and testable by the Specific Aims and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses should be narrow enough to be addressable by the proposed experiments and to tie aims together conceptually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess aims via reviewer-centered questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Start assessing your Specific Aims by taking a hard look at the significance and innovation of your planned research. Ask yourself: Would my reviewers see my proposed project as tackling an important problem? Would they view my Specific Aims as capable of opening up new discoveries? Would my reviewers regard the work as new and unique? Would they view my Specific Aims as likely to exert a significant influence on the research field(s) involved? Are my Specific Aims written clearly and are they easy to understand?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist to judge aims from a reviewer’s perspective; clarity and perceived impact are critical to favorable review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get outside and expert feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: You'll want to get outside opinions for a fresh perspective. Don't assume others, including your reviewers, will consider a research area to have the same priority that you do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss aims with colleagues outside your field for clarity, and with colleagues who have NIH funding or study-section experience for relevance and competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame innovative/high-risk work carefully with supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis-driven research does not necessarily constrain paradigm-shifting or 'outside-the-box' research. For projects predominantly focused on innovation and outside-the-box research, investigators have options, but high-risk research is often difficult to succeed in review without sufficient supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your proposal challenges commonly held beliefs, include sufficient preliminary data to convince reviewers; make reviewers feel the risk is worth taking. Consider alternative mechanisms (R21, DP1, DP2) better suited for exploratory/high-risk work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility matters as much as novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Never forget that reviewers also look at the feasibility of the proposed research. Novelty alone will not help you if the proposed studies are not feasible given the available time, funds, and resources to do the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance innovation with realistic, feasible aims; clearly justify that the team and resources will permit successful completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate grant mechanism for fit
rubrics_metrics.description: For projects focused on innovation and outside-the-box research, investigators always have the option to use grant mechanisms other than R01s (e.g., R21, DP1, DP2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the mechanism aligned with scope and risk level; high-risk, exploratory studies may be better submitted to mechanisms designed for those aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create aims with clear reviewer-assessable endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Your goal is to create aims that are achievable in four to five years and have clear endpoints your reviewers can readily assess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state expected outcomes, success/failure criteria, and measurable endpoints so reviewers can judge likely impact and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay in your niche to maximize impact and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Staying in your niche, propose a project that addresses a highly significant problem, is innovative, and is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrow, specialized proposals leveraging your background and niche expertise are more likely to be feasible and persuasive to study sections aligned with that niche.
